attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his December 2022 Substack post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will come... from' forecast, conditioned on AGI arriving ('when it does'), which is kept as a qualifier. The paraphrase drops 'explicit knowledge', but 'built-in knowledge' covers the point closely enough. No deadline.

contract.note: The plain reading (broadly capable, reliable, aligned AGI with disclosed architecture) is ordinary and fair. The evaluator's requirement for independent verification is an evidentiary step, not a stretch. Whether the claim can resolve depends on what counts as trustworthy AGI, a test Marcus did not define.

evidence.note: The Feb 2026 safety report describes ongoing reliability limits. It does not show that qualifying AGI exists or what architecture it has, so it cannot settle the forecast.

reviews.rationale: This forecast about AGI's architecture only becomes testable once trustworthy, aligned AGI exists and its architecture is disclosed. Nothing in the packet shows such a system by the evaluation date, so the early-resolution rule is not met. There is no deadline, and the absence of AGI is not a failure of the forecast. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, from his list of predictions about GPT-4.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' claim that some GPT-4 advice will exist that is head-scratchingly bad. 'Very bad' is a fair paraphrase. No deadline.

contract.note: Reading 'head-scratchingly bad' as seriously wrong or potentially harmful advice, judged by qualified evaluators, is an ordinary plain reading. It is not stretched for or against Marcus.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed study: infectious-disease physicians judged some ChatGPT-4 management plans harmful (7 of 44 overall). This is GPT-4 advice judged against clinical guidelines. The packet oddly lists it as counterevidence, but it supports the claim.

reviews.rationale: The claim only needs some bad advice to exist. A dated peer-reviewed study documents GPT-4 medical advice that specialists rated harmful, which meets the early-resolution rule. The good advice found in other cases does not cut against an 'at least some' forecast. Supported.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: 'If so, we can expect' is firm expectation, conditioned on GPT-4 being architecturally essentially the same as GPT-3. The antecedent and the causal link are both kept.

contract.note: Requiring the antecedent to be verified, plus evidence about internal representations, is fair. However, 'essentially the same architecture', 'world models' and 'abstract understanding' have no operational definitions, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: Researchers note that GPT-4's technical details are undisclosed. This leaves the antecedent unverified but does not show it is false.
Behavioural study of an early pre-release GPT-4 showing broad capabilities. It does not establish the released model's internal representations or its architecture.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent (architectural sameness with GPT-3) is not verified because GPT-4's architecture is undisclosed, and the policy says a conditional with an unknown antecedent is not scored. Even setting that aside, no evidence establishes or refutes internal world models in released GPT-4. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, part of his GPT-4 predictions.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' disjunction: GPT-4 will either refuse (under aggressive guardrails) or occasionally give plausible but dangerous medical nonsense. The guardrail condition and 'occasionally' are both preserved.

contract.note: Reading 'dangerous nonsense' as fluent answers that clinicians judge incorrect and potentially harmful is an ordinary reading. Satisfying one branch of the disclaimed either/or is enough, which is fair to the wording.

evidence.note: Same study: GPT-4 gave detailed, well-written answers to real medical cases, which shows the plausible-sounding part.
Specialists rated some of those fluent GPT-4 management plans harmful, which establishes the dangerous-answer branch.
A separate study found no majority-rated harmful GPT-4 answers. That bounds how often harm occurs but does not negate 'occasionally' in other settings.

reviews.rationale: A dated peer-reviewed clinical evaluation documents fluent GPT-4 answers to real medical queries, several of which specialists rated harmful. This meets the early-resolution rule for the 'occasional dangerous nonsense' branch. The study in e3 that found no harm limits frequency but does not refute an 'occasionally' claim. Supported.
